title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Reproducible Ceiling/Null Result
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) comparing a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline to accepting an LLM suggestion directly for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator we selected K=200 tasks by a reproducible SHA‑256 sorting rule and evaluated a single shared generator output per task. Observed primary outcome: baseline = 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10k, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair step was never invoked. The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis H1 (that G→V→R yields fewer regression‑causing changes than LLM‑only) was not supported under the tested model/validator/task selection regime. All execution and scoring artifacts are archived for replay (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6580c9df4...), and the exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). We interpret this as a ceiling/null result specific to the tested regime and provide artifact‑grounded guidance for designing future failure‑rich evaluations.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation can reduce operator effort but risks regressions (reachability or service loss). A canonical mitigation architecture is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): LLM proposes config, a deterministic verifier checks workflow and safety constraints, and a repair step attempts fixes before apply. Prior work advocates such pipelines and presents prototypes, but causal, preregistered estimates of verifier utility under reproducible conditions are scarce. We preregistered (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256 = a6d73a5cc0bda22e...) and executed a paired experiment that isolates the verifier+repair marginal effect by using a single shared generator output per task. Our primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (paired binary outcome). We report a fully archived, deterministic execution and its artifact‑grounded interpretation.
sections.related_work: Recent literature emphasizes generate–validate–repair and verifier‑assisted pipelines for NetOps and AIOps, and advocates integrating formal deterministics verifiers to bound LLM‑induced risk. Benchmarks and position papers (e.g., Cornetto and related generate–validate–repair studies) motivate our confirmatory design. Our contribution is a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired causal estimate that quantifies the verifier's marginal effect under a fixed generator output and preregistered sampling rule.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The preregistered plan (cand-002-gvr-loop; SHA‑256 a6d73a5c...) fixed: K=200 tasks; paired design; single shared_initial_generation per task (both arms used the same initial candidate); maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1; requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558ed...); deterministic task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task selection: deterministic SHA‑256(intent) sort and first 200 unique tasks (no human selection) — manifest archived at execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...). The inclusion rule required preregistered validator coverage, so every selected task satisfied the validator's declared coverage by construction. Execution and artifact capture. Every model prompt/response, provider call trace, validator trace, and scoring JSON was archived. Key artifact fingerprints: raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6..., execution/transformation_manifest.json SHA‑256 = 79c91155.... Analysis plan. Primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binaries; paired bootstrap (10k, seed=1729) percentile 95% CI. All analysis code and seeds archived; outputs archived (analysis/* SHA‑256s listed in manifest).
sections.results: Execution summary. Planned episodes: 400 (two arms × 200 tasks). Completed episodes: 400. Model calls used: 200 (one shared initial generator call per task; guard path allowed one repair call but none were invoked). Primary paired contingency (guarded × baseline): n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 7bc1bd2a...). Primary inferential outcome: paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10k, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 = 52a0858d...). Repair usage. The verifier never reported a failing initial candidate in any guarded episode; repair_applied=false in every execution/scoring/*.json. Representative diagnostics. Per‑task scoring JSONs contain validator diagnostics (parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, normalized_configuration, final_state snapshots). Example: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256 = 3055f874...) contains parsed_command_count=4 and validator.valid=true. Aggregated difficulty/coverage summary. By design all K=200 included tasks satisfied the preregistered validator coverage requirement (inclusion filter). A deterministic per‑task difficulty label (e.g., medium/hard/very_hard) is present in each execution/scoring/*.json; however, an aggregated count of those labels across the full K=200 sample was not produced by the autonomous analysis pipeline and therefore is not reported as a numeric table here. The raw per‑task difficulty metadata and validator coverage indicators are archived and reproducible at execution/scoring/*.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...); analysts can deterministically aggregate these JSONs to produce counts. Reproducibility pointers. Full replay artifacts: execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6...), execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = 1acce925...), execution/transformation_manifest.json (SHA‑256 = 79c91155...), and the master prompt provenance at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e...).
sections.discussion: Interpretation. The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis H1 (that G→V→R reduces regression‑causing applies vs LLM‑only) was not supported for the tested regime: no discordant pairs were observed and repairs were never exercised. This ceiling/null outcome is specific to the sampling contract (tasks filtered to validator‑covered intents), the chosen generator (requested gpt-5-mini), and the shared_initial_generation estimand that fixes generator output across arms. Design implications. To measure verifier utility in future confirmatory paired tests investigators should (1) ensure baseline failure prevalence by sampling failure‑rich historical or adversarial intents or by evaluating weaker generator configurations; (2) consider an interactive estimator where generators may adapt to validator feedback (closed‑loop regeneration) rather than fixing a shared initial candidate; and (3) publish per‑task validator coverage and difficulty aggregates alongside paired counts. Our archived artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl) enable deterministic reproduction of per‑task aggregates and replay of alternative estimands by allowing regeneration and additional model calls. Statistical note. The degenerate bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00] and McNemar p=1.00 correctly describe the observed sample; they do not imply general absence of verifier value in other sampling regimes.
sections.conclusion: Under a fully preregistered and archived paired design (K=200 tasks selected deterministically from validator‑covered intents, single shared generator candidate per task, requested_model=gpt-5-mini), we observed baseline = 200/200 validator‑compliant applies and guarded = 200/200, yielding a paired difference of 0.00 (McNemar p=1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]). The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis H1 was not supported in this tested regime. The repair pathway was never invoked. This outcome is a reproducible ceiling/null result under the stated constraints (all raw artifacts and hashes archived: raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6...; model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce9255...; master prompt provenance SHA‑256 = 1872df1e...). We recommend that future confirmatory evaluations intentionally sample failure‑rich tasks, vary generator strengths, or adopt interactive generator–verifier estimands to exercise repair logic and reveal verifier utility. All execution, scoring, and provenance artifacts are released for replay and independent audit (paths and SHA‑256 values listed in the Disclosure).

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (requested_model = gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments.

Task pool construction required preregistered validator coverage for inclusion; this design choice biased the sample toward intents the validator already supports and therefore reduces external validity to failure‑rich production distributions.
Construct validity depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity; validator blind spots would render the binary outcome an imperfect proxy for true operational regressions.

Shared_initial_generation fixes generator output across arms and prevents closed‑loop generator adaptation; the experiment therefore measures verifier marginality on fixed candidates rather than end‑to‑end adaptive improvement.
Observed ceiling (baseline success = 100%) made the preregistered power assumption inapplicable; inference is descriptive and bounded to the archived sampling/model regime.
